title: Light-activated LED
content_html:
Materials

  • 1 x Arduino Uno (or compatible) board (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x USB cable (A to B) for programming the Arduino (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x Breadboard (half-size or full-size) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Photoresistor / LDR (Light Dependent Resistor) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 10kΩ resistor (for the LDR voltage divider) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 1 x LED (any colour, 5mm standard) (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x 220Ω resistor (to protect the LED) (Nerokas - nerokas.co.ke)
  • 6–8 x Male-to-male jumper wires (Pixel Electronics - pixelelectronics.co.ke)
  • 1 x Small box, cloth, or hand to test "darkness" (no supplier needed)

How It Works

A photoresistor (also called an LDR, or Light Dependent Resistor) is a special component whose resistance changes depending on how much light hits it. In bright light, it lets electricity flow through easily (low resistance). In the dark, it blocks electricity much more (high resistance).

The Arduino cannot measure resistance directly, but it can measure voltage. So we build a simple circuit called a "voltage divider" — we connect the photoresistor and a fixed 10kΩ resistor in series, and we read the voltage at the point where they meet. When it's bright, more voltage appears at that point. When it's dark, the voltage at that point drops (or rises, depending on wiring orientation).

The Arduino reads this voltage using one of its analog input pins, which converts the voltage into a number between 0 and 1023. In our code, we check that number: if it crosses a certain "threshold" (a cut-off value we choose), the Arduino decides it is dark and turns the LED ON. If it's bright, the LED stays OFF. This is exactly how streetlights and some security lights work in real life — they sense darkness and switch themselves on automatically, without a human flicking a switch.

Step-by-Step Instructions

  1. Place the breadboard in front of you and insert the Arduino nearby, not yet connected to a computer.
  2. Insert the photoresistor into the breadboard so its two legs sit in two different rows.
  3. Connect one leg of the photoresistor to the Arduino's 5V pin using a jumper wire.
  4. Connect the 10kΩ resistor so that one end shares the same row as the other leg of the photoresistor, and the other end goes to the Arduino's GND pin. This creates the voltage divider.
  5. Run a jumper wire from the junction point (where the photoresistor and 10kΩ resistor meet) to analog pin A0 on the Arduino. This is the point whose voltage will change with light.
  6. Insert the LED into the breadboard, making sure students identify the longer leg (positive/anode) and shorter leg (negative/cathode).
  7. Connect the longer leg of the LED, through the 220Ω resistor, to digital pin 8 on the Arduino.
  8. Connect the shorter leg of the LED directly to GND on the Arduino.
  9. Double-check all connections against the circuit diagram before powering on — loose wires are the most common issue.
  10. Connect the Arduino to the computer with the USB cable and open the Arduino IDE.
  11. Type or paste the sketch from the "Full Code" section below, select the correct board and port, and click Upload.
  12. Once uploaded, open the Serial Monitor (set to 9600 baud) so students can see the live light-level readings scrolling by.
  13. Ask students to cover the photoresistor with their hand or a small box and observe: the number on the Serial Monitor should rise or fall, and the LED should turn ON.
  14. Ask students to uncover it and shine a phone torch directly on it — the LED should turn OFF and the reading should change back.
  15. Let each student experiment with covering/uncovering and discuss what they notice about the changing numbers.

Full Code


// Light-activated LED
// Reads a photoresistor voltage divider on A0
// Turns an LED on Pin 8 ON when it gets dark, OFF when bright

const int lightSensorPin = A0;   // Analog pin connected to the voltage divider junction
const int ledPin = 8;            // Digital pin connected to the LED (through 220 ohm resistor)

int darkThreshold = 500;         // Trial-and-error value: readings BELOW this mean "dark"
                                  // Increase this number if the LED turns on too easily
                                  // Decrease this number if the LED stays off in dim light

void setup() {
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);       // Tell Arduino the LED pin will send power out, not receive it
  Serial.begin(9600);            // Start serial communication so we can see readings on the computer
}

void loop() {
  int lightLevel = analogRead(lightSensorPin);  // Read voltage, gives a number from 0 (dark-ish) to 1023 (bright-ish)

  Serial.print("Light level: ");                // Print a label so the numbers make sense
  Serial.println(lightLevel);                   // Print the actual reading, then move to a new line

  if (lightLevel < darkThreshold) {              // If the reading is below our chosen cut-off...
    digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH);                  // ...it's dark, so turn the LED ON
  } else {
    digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);                   // Otherwise it's bright enough, so turn the LED OFF
  }

  delay(200);                                    // Wait briefly so readings don't scroll too fast to read
}

Common Mistakes & Fixes

Symptom Likely Cause Fix
LED stays on all the time, even in bright light darkThreshold value is set too high for the room's actual light level Watch the Serial Monitor numbers in bright light, then lower darkThreshold to just below that number
LED never turns on, even when fully covered darkThreshold value is set too low, or the photoresistor wiring is reversed Check the readings while covering the sensor; raise darkThreshold above the "dark" reading, and confirm wiring against the diagram
Serial Monitor shows nothing or garbled text Baud rate mismatch, or wrong port/board selected Set Serial Monitor baud rate to 9600 to match Serial.begin(9600); reselect the correct board/port in the IDE
LED does not light up at all, ever LED inserted backwards, or 220Ω resistor/wire not properly seated in breadboard Flip the LED so the longer leg (anode) goes toward the resistor and pin 8; push all wires firmly into the breadboard holes
Readings on Serial Monitor jump around wildly with no pattern Loose connection at the A0 junction, or photoresistor legs touching the wrong rows Re-seat the jumper wire at A0 and confirm the photoresistor and 10kΩ resistor share exactly one common row

Discussion Questions

  • What is a photoresistor, and how is its resistance different in light versus in darkness?
  • Why do we need a second resistor (the 10kΩ one) alongside the photoresistor to make this circuit work?
  • What does the number on the Serial Monitor actually represent, and why does it change?
  • Can you think of three real-world devices or places in Nairobi that might use a light sensor like this one?
  • If you wanted the LED to turn on only when it's very, very dark (not just dim), what would you change in the code?

Extension Challenges

  • Easy: Add a second LED that turns ON when it's bright (the opposite behaviour of the first LED), so one LED is always on at any given light level.
  • Medium: Replace the fixed darkThreshold with a calibration step — at the very start of the program, take a reading and set the threshold automatically based on the current light level, instead of typing in a fixed number.
  • Hard: Use analogWrite() to make the LED fade in smoothly as it gets darker (dimmer light, dimmer LED at first, fully bright LED once it's very dark), instead of a simple ON/OFF switch.
